## The question

[Calculus Question about Rolle’s Theorem pertaining to velocity and acceleration](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2543667/calculus-question-about-rolle-s-theorem-pertaining-to-velocity-and-acceleration), asked by [incogNICO](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/508402/incognico) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-11-29; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> At 9:13 A.M., a sports car is traveling 35 miles per hour. Two minutes later, the car is traveling 85 miles per hour. Prove that at some time during this two-minute interval, the car’s acceleration is exactly 1500 miles per hour squared.
:::

The [Mean Value Theorem][1] states that if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then there exists a point $c$ in $(a,b)$ such that 
$$\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b-a} = f'(c)$$
If you think of $f$ as varying over time, the left-hand side is the average rate of change of $f$ over the interval $[a,b]$, and the right-hand side is the instantaneous rate of change at $c$.  

You mentioned Rolle's Theorem in your title; the MVT is equivalent to it.

If $f$ is velocity, what is $f'$?

  [1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem
